Streaming Token Budgets

By Dana Whitfield · March 14, 2026 · 9 min read

Every tool call that returns a web page spends context. When an agent reads three documentation pages in a row, the raw HTML for each one can easily consume more tokens than the question that started the investigation. The fix is not to read less; it is to read the same page with less noise.

This note describes the budget model we settled on after watching a week of traces. The model has three parts: a main-content extractor, a hard token budget per read, and a local cache keyed by normalized URL.

Why extraction beats truncation

Truncation is the cheapest possible policy: read the first N characters and stop. It fails in a specific, expensive way — the first ten thousand characters of a real page are usually navigation, cookie banners, and a table of contents, so the model pays for chrome and still misses the answer in section six.

Extraction inverts that. We score candidate containers by text length, subtract link text, and nudge the score by class and id names. Readers whose content lives inside <article> or <main> skip the scoring entirely. What survives is the prose, the code, the lists, and the tables.

A budget you can continue

A budget that silently drops the tail is worse than no budget, because the model cannot tell whether it saw everything. So a truncated read ends with an explicit marker that names the token count of the whole document and the offset to resume from:

{
  "truncated": true,
  "nextOffset": 4820,
  "content": "...[truncated: full text 12040 chars]"
}

The rules we follow when cutting:

  • Cut on a paragraph boundary when one is available in the last 40% of the window.
  • Never cut inside a fenced code block; close the fence if the cut lands mid-block.
  • Always report both the delivered size and the size of the whole document.

Cache the result, not the bytes

The cache stores the extracted markdown rather than the raw response. Extraction is deterministic, so caching its output is safe, and a hit then saves network, parsing, and rendering in one step. Keys include an extractor version so that improving the extractor invalidates old entries instead of quietly serving yesterday's algorithm.

PolicyTokens per readNotes
Raw HTML31,400Baseline, unusable
Full-text markdown8,100Keeps all chrome
Extracted + budget1,350This note

A budget without a continuation marker is a lie with good manners.

What we deliberately skip

Comments, related-post rails, breadcrumbs, pagination, share buttons, and newsletter prompts are dropped unconditionally when their class or id names them. Article headers are kept when they carry real text, because the byline and the date are frequently the reason the page was fetched at all.

None of this changes the underlying fetch. The provider still owns DNS policy, timeouts, redirect limits, and decoding; the plugin only decides what the model is allowed to pay for.
